QUESTION OF THE WEEK - After the favourable "living wage" outcome and low inflation of the last week, there has been some increased talk about the chance of a rate cut.

Economists were asked about their outlook for interest rates, and the events of the past week have had little impact on their expectations. Two weeks ago, the median forecast was a 25 percent chance of a rate cut, with a range of forecasts from zero to 50 percent.

At the end of last week, the median forecast was a 27.5 percent chance of a rate cut, with a range of five to 50 percent. While slightly higher, economists said the wage outcome and inflation data was largely in line with forecasts and so had little effect.

This week is expected to restore some confidence to the rates-on-hold case, with two activity indicators -- building approvals and retail trade -- both expected to show signs of improving growth through 1997.

The major concern remains the stagnant labour market. If it remains weak, and there is renewed weakness in other indicators, then a cut could be on the cards. One thing economists agree on is that inflation is not standing in the way of a rate cut.

BALANCE ON GOODS AND SERVICES - After an unexpectedly strong performance in February, the surplus is seen narrowing in March. Rural exports have risen in each of the last four months and total exports have risen 14.4 percent in the last four months, so some analysts are looking for a correction there. Both the market and analysts are still getting used to this figure.

WAGES -- The impact of this figure is difficult to ascertain, and will depend on the market's sentiment ahead of the figures. While the quarterly growth will show a moderation, and probably be the lowest figure for a year, because it replaces a low 0.4 percent first quarter rise last year, the annual rate is expected to rise above four percent. However, as private sector AWOTE is running around 3.0 percent, and with structural adjustments in the public sector seen pushing AWOTE up there, the general expectation is that a figure near the median should be well received, especially in light of the "living wage" decision.

BUILDING APPROVALS - A volatile monthly series, a small rise is generally expected, consistent with expectations of an improving housing sector. Among those at the higher end of forecasts, there was some talk of a large Sydney inner-city medium density development having been approved, as well as some who were also expecting an impact from the Olympic village to be seen in the data.
RETAIL TRADE - A strong figure here, especially if it

follows a larger than expected wages number, may put some serious dents in the rate cut case. While the impact of Easter falling in March was unclear, over the quarter real retail trade is expected to have risen strongly, after a weak December

quarter. Economists said it would probably contribute around 0.5 to 0.6 percentage points to GDP, and combined with a strong performance by motor registrations, pointed to very strong private consumption.
